summary: An island nation in the north-central Indian Ocean made up of about 1,200 coral islands, the smallest country in Asia by area and the lowest in average elevation, known for its resort islands.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: After the king converted to Islam in 1153, Islam became the state religion of the Maldives, and Buddhist monasteries were demolished or converted. Successive sultans afterward used Islam to hold the society of the islands together; the 2008 constitution provides that only Muslims can be citizens, and the public practice of other religions is restricted by law, so almost all citizens are Sunni Muslims.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are mainly foreign workers from India, employed in tourist resorts, medicine, education and other sectors. Because Maldivian law prohibits the public practice of non-Islamic religions, they can only perform religious rituals in private places.

ranking.name: Other (Buddhism, Christianity, etc.)
ranking.description: Buddhists are mainly foreign workers from Sri Lanka and other Asian countries, and Christians include migrant workers and foreign professionals from India, the Philippines and elsewhere. Maldivian law prohibits public activity and proselytizing by non-Islamic religions.

religion.background: The early inhabitants of the Maldives probably came from Sri Lanka and southern India, and before Islamization they were Buddhists for more than a thousand years, and the islands retain the remains of stupas and monasteries. In 1153 King Dhovemi converted to Islam, reportedly influenced by a Muslim traveler from North Africa or Persia, and Islam became the state religion thereafter. In the 16th century the Portuguese briefly occupied Malé, and in 1573 Muhammad Thakurufaanu led his people in expelling the Portuguese and is honored as a national hero. From 1887 to 1965 the Maldives was a British protectorate, and in 1968 it became a republic. The 2008 constitution provides that all citizens must be Muslims, and Islam is the foundation of national identity.

ranking.name: Dhivehi
ranking.description: Dhivehi is the mother tongue of the Maldivians, related to Sinhala, but over centuries of Islamization and island isolation it developed a distinctive character, written in the Thaana script. The constitution makes Dhivehi the national language, and since the citizens are almost all Maldivians, it is the language of the great majority.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English began to enter government during the British protectorate period (1887–1965), and from the 1960s the Maldives gradually made English the language of school instruction. After the first resort opened in 1972 tourism rose, and English is widely used in resorts, government and business, but few people have English as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: Bengali
ranking.description: Bengali speakers are mainly foreign workers from Bangladesh, who work in construction, cleaning and resort services and are one of the largest foreign worker groups in the Maldives; some have no legal status, and their living conditions have also drawn international attention.

language.history: Dhivehi belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European language family and is most closely related to Sinhala of Sri Lanka, indicating that the early migrants to the Maldives may have come from Sri Lanka. In ancient times it was written in the "Evela Akuru" script derived from Brahmi, and after Islamization it absorbed a large number of Arabic words. Around the 16th–17th centuries the distinctive Thaana script developed, written from right to left, with some letter shapes derived from Arabic numerals. During the British protectorate of 1887–1965, English entered government and education. Today Dhivehi is the national language, and English is the language of instruction from secondary school upward.

ranking.name: Mas huni (tuna and coconut salad)
ranking.description: Tuna (mostly smoked or canned) mixed with grated coconut, onion, chili and lime juice, eaten for breakfast with roshi flatbread.
ranking.history: Mas huni is the most typical Maldivian breakfast, reflecting the island nation's two great products: tuna and coconut. Maldivians have caught tuna by the traditional pole-and-line method for hundreds of years, and smoked and dried tuna (Maldive fish) was already an important export to Sri Lanka and southern India in the Middle Ages, which the 14th-century traveler Ibn Battuta also recorded.

ranking.name: Garudhiya (tuna broth)
ranking.description: A clear fish soup made by boiling fresh tuna with water and salt, eaten with rice, lime, chili and onion. The broth is light and sweetly savory, emphasizing the natural flavor of the tuna.
ranking.history: Garudhiya is regarded as the national soup of the Maldives and for hundreds of years has been the everyday food of fishing families. In the past Maldivians' daily meals revolved almost entirely around tuna, and making soup directly from the fresh fish caught that day was the simplest and most basic way of cooking. The concentrated fish broth can be further simmered into rihaakuru fish paste for preservation.

ranking.name: Gulha (tuna fritters)
ranking.description: Small round balls of dough filled with smoked tuna, coconut, onion and chili, deep-fried until golden. The crust is crisp, and the filling has the aroma of coconut and chili.
ranking.history: Gulha is the most popular of the Maldivian "short eats" (hedhikaa), small snacks taken with tea in the afternoon. Maldivians have the habit of drinking tea in the afternoon with various savory and sweet snacks, which is related to the influence of the British protectorate period and South Asian tea-drinking culture. At the breaking of the fast during Ramadan, gulha is also a common snack on the table.

ranking.name: Rihaakuru (tuna paste)
ranking.description: A dark brown, thick fish paste made by simmering tuna broth for a long time until concentrated, with a strong salty flavor, eaten with rice or flatbread. It has a rich taste, and a small amount adds savoriness to a meal.
ranking.history: Rihaakuru is the traditional way Maldivians preserve the essence of tuna. In the era before refrigerators, when there was too much catch, people kept simmering the cooking broth into a thick fish paste that could be kept for months or even longer. It is regarded as a unique Maldivian seasoning and is one of the tastes of home that Maldivians abroad miss most.

ranking.name: Roshi (flatbread)
ranking.description: A thin round bread made from flour, water and coconut oil, cooked on a griddle, similar to Indian roti. It has a soft texture and is often used to wrap mas huni or curry.
ranking.history: Roshi derives from the South Asian flatbread (roti) and came through the long-standing trade between the Maldives and India and Sri Lanka. Because the Maldives' coral islands are unsuited to growing wheat, flour has to be imported, but the flatbread has nevertheless blended into the local diet and become the daily breakfast staple eaten with mas huni.
